before: new URL(relative, base) resolves a relative reference against an absolute base and returns a URL object. new URL(absolute) parses an absolute URL. These calls do not open a network connection. The fixed example.invalid host is only data here.

url.searchParams is a URLSearchParams object. set(name, value) replaces that name’s existing values; append(name, value) adds another entry without removing earlier ones. Both mutate the parameters and return undefined. Spaces serialize as + in this query format, while a slash inside a value is encoded rather than becoming URL structure.

Parsing or encoding a URL does not approve its destination or scheme. Real applications need an explicit destination policy before navigation or requests. Optional practice: replace an existing query name using set and contrast it with append; do not concatenate unchecked data into structural separators.
after:
`new URL(path, base)` combines a path with a full base address. `new URL(address)` reads a full address on its own.

These calls build or read an address. They do not visit it. Our example uses the placeholder host `example.invalid`.

`url.searchParams` holds the address's query parameters: named values after the question mark.

`set(name, value)` replaces that name's values. `append(name, value)` adds another value, keeping earlier ones.

The URL tools encode special characters. A space becomes `+` here, and a slash inside a value becomes `%2F`.

Complete `topicURL(topic, tags)`. Set the topic once, then append each tag and return `url.href`.

Use the URL tools so characters such as `&` stay part of a value. This function only builds an address; it sends no request. Building a valid address alone does not make an unknown destination trustworthy.
